blocks.title: Internal energy
blocks.text: The sum of all forms of molecular energies (kinetic and potential) of a substance is termed its internal energy. In the study of thermodynamics an ideal gas is usually considered the working substance; the molecules of an ideal gas are mere mass points which exert no forces on one another, so the internal energy of an ideal gas system is generally the translational KE of its molecules. Since the temperature of a system is defined as the average KE of its molecules, for an ideal gas the internal energy is directly proportional to its temperature.

According to the kinetic theory of gases the average kinetic energy of gas molecules is given by the average of (1/2) m v^2 = (3/2) k_B T, where k_B is the Boltzmann constant. Therefore the rise in temperature of an object reflects an increase in the internal kinetic energy of its particles. This increase in internal energy can occur due to the absorption of heat energy, which raises the average kinetic energy of the particles and thus increases the temperature of the object.

A diatomic gas molecule has both translational and rotational energy; it also has vibrational energy associated with the spring-like bond between its atoms (Do You Know). Different processes can lead to changes in internal energy and temperature, such as heating (adding heat), adiabatic compression or expansion (no heat exchange), or phase changes, where heat energy changes the state of matter without changing temperature (Tidbits). Internal energy is a function of state: it does not depend on the path but on the initial and final states of the system; thus internal energy is similar to gravitational PE, and like potential energy it is the change in internal energy and not its absolute value which is important (For Your Information).

blocks.prompt: What is meant by internal energy, and how is it related to the temperature of an ideal gas (short question 6.2; MCQ 6.7)?
blocks.explanation: Internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy of all the molecules of a substance. For an ideal gas there is no molecular potential energy, so U is the total translational kinetic energy, which is (3/2) k_B T per molecule on average; U is therefore directly proportional to the absolute temperature, and a rise in temperature means a rise in internal energy.

items: Internal energy = all molecular KE + PE; for an ideal gas only translational KE, average (1/2) m v^2 = (3/2) k_B T, so U is proportional to T. A state function: only delta U matters. Heating, adiabatic changes and phase changes alter it.
